title: Oracle Function Based Index: Examples and Why It's Not Used
description: Create an Oracle function based index for UPPER, TRUNC and CASE, check it in the plan, and fix the common reasons Oracle ignores it.

sources.title: Oracle 19c SQL Language Reference: CREATE INDEX
Oracle 19c Concepts: Indexes and Index-Organized Tables
Oracle 19c SQL Tuning Guide: Optimizer Access Paths

reviewNotes: Examples written from the Oracle 19c docs; none were run, so all need a test run. Please verify: (1) exact COLUMN_EXPRESSION text in USER_IND_EXPRESSIONS, especially TRUNC(INTERNAL_FUNCTION(...)) for the DATE column, which is from memory, not the docs; (2) the DISPLAY_CURSOR plan shape and predicate text (needs a bigger table, see the note callout); (3) that creating ord_one_pending_ux while ord_pending_ix exists fails as the text implies, and that the ORA-00001 message format is right; (4) the hidden column naming SYS_NC... in USER_TAB_COLS; (5) FAQ claim that QUERY REWRITE privilege is not needed on current releases (based on its absence from the 19c CREATE INDEX prerequisites); (6) the FUNCIDX_STATUS column in USER_INDEXES. (7) the claim that a default GATHER_TABLE_STATS also gathers stats on the hidden SYS_NC virtual column.

data.text: An Oracle function based index stores the result of an expression, such as UPPER(customer_email) or TRUNC(order_date), instead of the raw column value. You create it with a normal CREATE INDEX statement that names the expression: CREATE INDEX ord_email_ix ON orders (UPPER(customer_email));. The optimizer can then use it for any query whose WHERE clause contains the same expression.

This tutorial shows how to create one, how to check that Oracle actually uses it, how to index only some rows, how to enforce a conditional unique rule, and the reasons a function based index is ignored. All examples use one small orders table that you can build in your own schema.
What is a function based index in Oracle?

A normal B-tree index stores column values. If your query wraps that column in a function, for example WHERE UPPER(customer_email) = ..., the stored values no longer match what you are searching for. Oracle cannot use the plain index for that predicate, so it usually reads the whole table.

A function based index fixes this by computing the expression once, when the row is inserted or updated, and storing the result in the index. Oracle's documentation describes it as an index that computes the value of a function or expression involving one or more columns and stores it. It can be a B-tree or a bitmap index.
The expression can be:

items.content: A built-in SQL function, such as UPPER, LOWER, TRUNC or SUBSTR.
An arithmetic expression, such as quantity * unit_price.
A CASE expression.
Your own PL/SQL function, as long as it is declared DETERMINISTIC.

data.text: Behind the scenes Oracle adds a hidden virtual column to the table to represent the expression, and the index is built on that column. You will see this hidden column later when we look at the data dictionary.
Sample setup

Create a small orders table. Emails are stored in mixed case on purpose, and order dates include a time part, because those are the two situations where developers most often reach for a function based index.

data.caption: Sample orders table

data.text: With only six rows the optimizer will often prefer a full table scan, because reading one or two blocks is cheaper than any index. To see index access in the plans below, load more rows first, for example with an INSERT ... SELECT that uses CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 100000, then gather statistics. The plan shapes shown here assume a table of that size.
Example 1: case-insensitive search with UPPER
Users type emails in any case. The usual query converts both sides to upper case:

data.caption: Case-insensitive lookup

data.code:
ORDER_ID CUSTOMER_EMAIL
-------- ------------------------
       1 Ravi.Kumar@example.com
       3 RAVI.KUMAR@EXAMPLE.COM
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The result is correct, but an ordinary index on customer_email cannot help, because the index holds Ravi.Kumar@example.com while the query looks for the upper-case form. Oracle has to apply UPPER to every row.
Step 1: create the index

data.code:
CREATE INDEX ord_email_upper_ix
  ON orders (UPPER(customer_email));
data.caption: Function based index on UPPER(customer_email)

data.text: Step 2: gather statistics

The Oracle SQL reference says to collect statistics on both the index and its base table with DBMS_STATS after creating a function based index, so the optimizer can decide correctly when to use it. Gathering table statistics also collects statistics for the hidden virtual column.

data.code:
BEGIN
  DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS(
    ownname => USER,
    tabname => 'ORDERS',
    cascade => TRUE);
END;
/
data.caption: Refresh table, column and index statistics

data.text: Step 3: confirm the plan

Run the query again and display the plan of the last statement in your session. In SQL*Plus or SQLcl, run SET SERVEROUTPUT OFF first, otherwise the last statement is the DBMS_OUTPUT call and not your query.

data.caption: Show the actual plan

data.code:
| Id | Operation                           | Name               |
|  0 | SELECT STATEMENT                    |                    |
|  1 |  TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID BATCHED| ORDERS             |
|* 2 |   INDEX RANGE SCAN                  | ORD_EMAIL_UPPER_IX |

Predicate Information (identified by operation id):
   2 - access(UPPER("CUSTOMER_EMAIL")='RAVI.KUMAR@EXAMPLE.COM')
data.caption: Output (expected output, cost columns removed)

data.text: The INDEX RANGE SCAN on ORD_EMAIL_UPPER_IX and the access predicate tell you the index was used to find the rows. If you see TABLE ACCESS FULL with a filter predicate instead, the index was not used. If you are new to plans, read how to read an explain plan in Oracle first.
Example 2: search by day with TRUNC(order_date)
A DATE column in Oracle always carries a time. A common report query asks for all orders placed on one day:

data.caption: Index and query on the day part of a DATE
Output (expected output, NLS_DATE_FORMAT set to YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS)

data.text: Both rows from 21 October are returned, including the one at 23:55. The index stores midnight of each date, so the equality search matches exactly.

If you already have a plain index on order_date, you often do not need a second one. Rewrite the filter as a range: WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-10-21' AND order_date < DATE '2026-10-22'. That uses the existing index and saves the cost of maintaining another one.
Example 3: index an expression across columns
The expression can combine several columns. Suppose a dashboard often looks for large orders by line value:

data.caption: Index on an arithmetic expression

data.text: Oracle matches the query to the index by comparing expression trees. According to the Oracle Concepts guide, this comparison is case-insensitive and ignores blank spaces, so QUANTITY*UNIT_PRICE matches too. It is not a general algebra engine, though. Writing unit_price * quantity is a different expression, so keep the query in the same form as the index definition.
Example 4: index only some rows
Oracle does not store a B-tree index entry when every key column is NULL. You can use that to build a small index that covers only the rows you care about. Here only pending orders get an entry:

data.caption: Partial index using CASE

data.code:
ORDER_ID CUSTOMER_ID
-------- -----------
       2         102
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Shipped and cancelled orders map to NULL, so they never enter the index. If most orders are shipped, this index stays tiny and cheap to maintain, while the work queue query stays fast. The trade-off is that the query must repeat the exact CASE expression, which is easy to forget. A view or a virtual column (see below) hides that detail.
Example 5: enforce a conditional unique rule
A unique function based index can enforce a rule that a normal constraint cannot express. For example: a customer may have many orders, but at most one PENDING order at a time.

data.code:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ord_one_pending_ux
  ON orders (CASE status WHEN 'PENDING' THEN customer_id END);
data.caption: At most one pending order per customer

data.text: Create this instead of ord_pending_ix from Example 4, not as well. Oracle allows more than one index on the same expression only in limited cases, such as a different index type, and only one of them can be visible. Now try to add a second pending order for customer 102:

data.code: INSERT INTO orders VALUES (7, 102, 'priya.n@example.com', SYSDATE, 'PENDING', 1, 500.00);
data.caption: Second pending order for the same customer

data.code: ORA-00001: unique constraint (YOUR_SCHEMA.ORD_ONE_PENDING_UX) violated
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The insert fails because customer 102 already has order 2 in PENDING status. Inserting a SHIPPED order for the same customer works, because its index key is NULL and is not stored. Oracle's own CREATE INDEX documentation uses this same technique to allow a promotion only once per customer.
Example 6: a user-defined function in the index

You can index your own PL/SQL function, but Oracle requires it to be declared DETERMINISTIC. That keyword is a promise that the same inputs always return the same output. Oracle relies on that promise, it does not verify it.

data.caption: Deterministic function and its index
Query that can use ord_domain_ix

data.code:
ORDERS_FROM_DOMAIN
------------------
                 6
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: If you leave out DETERMINISTIC, the CREATE INDEX fails with ORA-30553: The function is not deterministic. Two more rules from the Oracle docs: the index owner needs EXECUTE privilege on the function, and if the function becomes invalid or is dropped, Oracle marks the index DISABLED.

Never mark a function DETERMINISTIC if its result depends on table data, SYSDATE, session settings or package variables. Oracle will store whatever the function returned at insert time, and later queries through the index can return wrong results. After you change the logic of an indexed function, rebuild the index.
Why is my function based index not being used?
This is the most common question about function based indexes. Work through these checks in order.
1. The query expression does not match the index

The predicate must contain the same expression. An index on UPPER(customer_email) does not help LOWER(customer_email) = ..., customer_email = ... or UPPER(TRIM(customer_email)) = .... To see exactly what Oracle stored, query the dictionary:

data.caption: See the stored index expressions

data.code:
INDEX_NAME          COLUMN_EXPRESSION
------------------- --------------------------------------------
ORD_EMAIL_UPPER_IX  UPPER("CUSTOMER_EMAIL")
ORD_DAY_IX          TRUNC(INTERNAL_FUNCTION("ORDER_DATE"))
ORD_VALUE_IX        "QUANTITY"*"UNIT_PRICE"
...
data.caption: Output (expected output, exact text can vary by version)

data.text: 2. Statistics are missing or stale

The hidden virtual column has its own column statistics. If the table was analysed before the index existed, the optimizer has no idea how selective the expression is and may guess badly. Gather table statistics again, as in Example 1. You can see the hidden column like this:

data.code:
SELECT column_name, hidden_column, virtual_column, data_default
  FROM user_tab_cols
 WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS'
   AND hidden_column = 'YES';
data.caption: List the hidden virtual columns

data.text: Each function based index appears as a row with a system-generated name that starts with SYS_NC and VIRTUAL_COLUMN = YES. You may also see that name in plan predicates.
3. Data type conversion changes the expression

If you compare a VARCHAR2 expression with a number, Oracle adds an implicit TO_NUMBER around the expression, and it no longer matches the index. The Oracle SQL Tuning Guide calls out this exact mistake with plain columns. Compare with a literal or bind of the same data type as the expression.
4. The optimizer thinks a full scan is cheaper

An index is only used when it is cheaper. If the predicate matches a large part of the table, or the table is tiny, a full scan wins and that is the right decision. Check the row estimate in the plan against the real count before assuming something is broken.
5. The index is disabled, unusable or invisible

data.caption: Check index state

data.text: FUNCIDX_STATUS shows DISABLED when the underlying function is invalid or was dropped. Recompile the function, then run ALTER INDEX ord_domain_ix ENABLE;. An INVISIBLE index is ignored unless OPTIMIZER_USE_INVISIBLE_INDEXES is TRUE for your session.
6. Queries that need every row

The Oracle docs note that the database will not use a function based index unless the query filters out nulls, for example an ORDER BY UPPER(customer_email) with no WHERE clause. Rows whose expression is NULL are missing from the index, so the index cannot return them. Adding a filter such as WHERE UPPER(customer_email) IS NOT NULL, or making sure the expression cannot be NULL, gives the optimizer that option.
Virtual column or function based index?

Oracle 11g and later let you add a virtual column and index it. The Oracle Administrator's Guide says an index on a virtual column is equivalent to a function based index. The difference is how you query it.

data.caption: The same idea as a named virtual column

data.text: Run this on a fresh copy of the table, or drop ord_email_upper_ix first, since both indexes cover the same expression.

content: None if queries already use the expression
Queries must use the new column name

data.text: Pick a function based index when you cannot change the SQL, for example a packaged application that already searches with UPPER. Pick a virtual column when you write the queries yourself and want one clear name for the derived value.
Common mistakes

items.content: Indexing one form and querying another. UPPER in the index, LOWER in the query. Agree on one form across the team and in your ORM settings.
Forgetting to gather statistics after creating the index on a table that already has data.
Marking a function DETERMINISTIC when it is not, which can give wrong query results.
Using SYSDATE, USER or ROWNUM in the expression. Oracle rejects them because they do not return a repeatable value.
Creating many expression indexes on a busy table. Every INSERT and every UPDATE of the involved columns must evaluate each expression and maintain each index.
Adding TRUNC indexes when a range predicate would do. See the tip in Example 2.

data.text: Performance tips

items.content: Index an expression only when queries filter on it often and the filter is selective. Check real plans with DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR before and after.
Use CASE expressions that return NULL for uninteresting rows to keep the index small.
Keep user-defined functions in indexes simple and fast, because they run on every insert and on updates to their input columns.
On a busy production table, consider CREATE INDEX ... ONLINE so DML can continue while the index builds.
Use an invisible index to test a new function based index before the whole application sees it.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is a function based index in Oracle with example?

It is an index on the result of an expression rather than on a raw column. Example: CREATE INDEX emp_upper_ix ON employees (UPPER(last_name)); lets WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'KING' use an index range scan.
Can a function based index have multiple columns?
Yes. The expression can use several columns, such as quantity * unit_price, and the index can mix expressions and plain columns, such as (UPPER(last_name), department_id).
Does a function based index store NULL values?

A B-tree function based index does not store rows where all key values are NULL. That is why queries that must return every row, including NULL results, cannot rely on it, and why the CASE trick in Example 4 works.
Why is my function based index disabled?
Oracle marks it DISABLED when the function it depends on becomes invalid or is dropped. Fix and recompile the function, then run ALTER INDEX ... ENABLE.
Do I need the QUERY REWRITE privilege for a function based index?

Not in current releases. The Oracle 19c CREATE INDEX prerequisites list only the normal index privileges, DETERMINISTIC for user-defined functions, and EXECUTE on those functions for the index owner. Very old releases had extra requirements.
Summary

items.content: A function based index stores the result of an expression, so queries filtering on that expression can use an index.
Create it with CREATE INDEX ... ON table (expression) and gather statistics afterwards.
The query must use the same expression as the index; check USER_IND_EXPRESSIONS.
User-defined functions must be DETERMINISTIC and really be deterministic.
Use CASE expressions that return NULL to index only some rows or to enforce conditional uniqueness.
Confirm usage with DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR, and consider a virtual column when you control the SQL.

linkedin.post:
Your index on customer_email exists, yet WHERE UPPER(customer_email) = '...' still does a full table scan.

The reason: a normal index stores the raw value, not UPPER of it. Oracle cannot use it once you wrap the column in a function.

The fix is a function based index:
→ CREATE INDEX ord_email_ix ON orders (UPPER(customer_email));
→ Gather table stats afterwards so the optimizer knows about the hidden virtual column behind it.
→ The query must use the same expression. An UPPER index does nothing for LOWER(customer_email).
→ A CASE expression that returns NULL for most rows gives you a small index on just the rows you need, such as pending orders.
→ A UNIQUE index on CASE status WHEN 'PENDING' THEN customer_id END allows only one pending order per customer.

Your own PL/SQL function can be indexed too, but it must be DETERMINISTIC, and it must really return the same output for the same input.

Which do you prefer for case-insensitive search in Oracle: a function based index or a virtual column?
